'''Héctor Daniel Abruña''' (born on November 8<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 7, 2024 |title=Héctor D. Abruña (USA) 2024 |url=https://globalenergyprize.org/en/2024/07/10/hector-d-abruna-usa-2024/}}</ref> 1953) is a Puerto Rican [[Physical chemistry|physical chemist]] whose work focuses on [[electrochemistry]], molecular electronics, fuel cells, batteries, and electrocatalysis. Abruña is director of the ''Energy Materials Center'' and Emile M. Chamot professor for chemistry at [[Cornell University]]. He became a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 2006,<ref name="AAAS 2006" /> a Member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2007,<ref name="AmAcad" /> and a Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2018.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/hector-d-abruna-wuw6jk/|title=NAS - Hector Abruna|publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]]|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref> Abruña conducts research into battery and fuel cell systems using electrochemical techniques and X-ray microscopy and spectroscopy methods.<ref name="NAS Cornell Chronicle" />

== Early life and education ==

Abruña was born in [[Santurce, San Juan, Puerto Rico]], in 1953<ref name=vitae>{{cite web|url=https://ecommons.cornell.edu/bitstream/handle/1813/3525/5_H%3Fctor_D_Abru%3Fa.pdf|title=Professor Héctor D. Abruña|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref> and grew up in Puerto Rico.<ref name="Cornell Sun NAS" /> He studied at [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]] in [[Troy, New York]], graduating with his bachelor of science degree in 1975 and master of science degree in 1976. He then earned a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in analytical chemistry at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] in 1980 under the direction of Thomas Meyer. As a postdoc, Abruña worked with [[Allen J. Bard]] at [[University of Texas at Austin]].<ref name=vitae/>

== Career ==

In 1982, Abruña became a professor at the [[University of Puerto Rico]].<ref name="Cornell Sun NAS" />
He joined the faculty at [[Cornell University]] in 1983.<ref name="Bard Award AS Cornell" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ise-online.org/portaits/AWARDS2016/CV_Abruna.pdf|title=Héctor D. Abruña|access-date=April 25, 2020}}</ref>

Abruña chaired the Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology 2004–2008.<ref name="Bard Award 235th ECS" />
He is director of the Energy Materials Center at Cornell (previously the Cornell Fuel Cell Institute).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.emc2.cornell.edu/members/category/leadership-team-1.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100718142224/http://www.emc2.cornell.edu/members/category/leadership-team-1.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 18, 2010|title=Energy Materials Center at Cornell - Leadership Team|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2003-11/cuns-mi110503.php|title=$2.25 million institute for fuel cell development|publisher=EurekAlert!, [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|AAAS]]|date=November 5, 2003|access-date=April 25, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/blog/2009/11/19/chair-sutley-visits-cornell-fuel-cell-institute-and-energy-materials-center|title=Chair Sutley Visits Cornell Fuel Cell Institute and Energy Materials Center|date=November 19, 2009|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref>
In 2018, Abruña became the lead of the Center for Alkaline-Based Energy Solutions (CABES) at Cornell University, supported by the [[United States Department of Energy]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2018/07/1075m-grant-aids-next-gen-fuel-cell-development|title=$10.75M grant aids next-gen fuel cell development|publisher=[[Cornell Chronicle]]}}</ref>

Abruña was co-chair of the ''Basic Energy Sciences Workshop on Electrical Energy Storage''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Abruña |first=Héctor D. |last2=Buchanan |first2=Michelle V. |last3=Goodenough |first3=John B. |date=2007 |title=Basic Research Needs for Electrical Energy Storage. Report of the Basic Energy Sciences Workshop on Electrical Energy Storage, April 2-4, 2007 |url=https://www.academia.edu/55166123/Basic_Research_Needs_for_Electrical_Energy_Storage_Report_of_the_Basic_Energy_Sciences_Workshop_on_Electrical_Energy_Storage_April_2_4_2007 |doi=10.2172/935429}}</ref> hosted by the [[United States Department of Energy]] in 2007 and acted as a principal editor on the report ''Basic Research Needs for Electrical Energy Storage''.<ref>{{cite tech report |title=Basic Research Needs for Electrical Energy Storage. Report of the Basic Energy Sciences Workshop on Electrical Energy Storage, April 2-4, 2007 |osti=935429 |osti-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/doi/10.1063/1.3047681|title=Batteries and electrochemical capacitors|journal=[[Physics Today]]|date=December 1, 2008|doi=10.1063/1.3047681|access-date=April 25, 2020|last1=Abruña|first1=Héctor D.|last2=Kiya|first2=Yasuyuki|last3=Henderson|first3=Jay C.|volume=61|issue=12|pages=43–47|bibcode=2008PhT....61l..43A|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
He chaired the 2006 Electrochemistry [[Gordon Research Conferences|Gordon Research Conference]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.grc.org/electrochemistry-conference/2006/|title=2006 Electrochemistry Conference GRC|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref> supported through the [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] and [[United States Department of Energy|DOE]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=0618126|title=Award Abstract #0618126 - Support for 2006 Electrochemistry Gordon Conference, Santa Ynez, California, February 12-17, 2006|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.osti.gov/biblio/901626|title=2006 Electrochemistry Gordon Research Conference - February 12-17-2006|first=Hector D.|last=Abruna|date=April 3, 2007|osti=901626 |via=www.osti.gov}}</ref>

Abruña advocates for underrepresented minorities to join the sciences at Cornell, and actively recruits students from Puerto Rican universities to access research and mentors in the Cornell High Energy Synchrotron Source.<ref name="CHESS hispanic-serving">{{cite web|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2018/10/hispanic-serving-institutions-partner-chess|title=Hispanic-serving institutions partner with CHESS|publisher=[[Cornell Chronicle]]|date=October 25, 2018|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://pages.uoregon.edu/coach/COACh_2015/2008_NSF-NIH-DoE_Workshop_Chemistry_Racial_Ethnic_Equity.pdf|title=Workshop on Excellence Empowered by a Diverse Academic Workforce: Achieving Racial & Ethnic Equity in Chemistry|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref>
Fifteen of the 55 students who graduated from Abruña's group as of 2018 were from Puerto Rico.<ref name="CHESS hispanic-serving" />
He collaborates on outreach activities with [[Casa Pueblo]] in [[Adjuntas, Puerto Rico]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=0847926|title=Award Abstract #0847926 - CCI Phase I: Center for Molecular Interfacing|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{YouTube|id=zZ-jWF83kqw|title=Institute for Functional Nanomaterials (IFN) 2009 - Broader Impacts part 1 of 2}}, {{YouTube|id=D0H-zRVM3Es|title=Institute for Functional Nanomaterials (IFN) 2009 - Broader Impacts part 2 of 2}}</ref>

Abruña co-founded the battery company Lionano in 2013, with an initial grant from PowerBridgeNY.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lionano.com/about|title=Next-Generation Battery Technology - Lionano - About Lionano|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://waveep.com/news/lionano-co-founder-and-chief-scientific-advisor-prof-hector-abruna-elected-member-of-the-national-academy-of-sciences/|title=Lionano Co-Founder and Chief Scientific Advisor, Prof. Héctor Abruña, Elected Member of the National Academy of Sciences|date=May 2018 |access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://powerbridgeny.com/awardees/24/|title=Lionano - PowerBridgeNY|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2016/10/07/the-case-for-the-icar-why-an-apple-car-isnt-crazy.html|title=The case for the iCar: Why an Apple car isn't crazy|publisher=[[CNBC]]|date=October 7, 2016|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref>
He also co-founded the startup company Ecolectro with [[Geoffrey W. Coates]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ecolectro.com|title=Ecolectro|access-date=April 25, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://nexus-ny.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/10/NewEnergy_Final_Web.pdf|title=New Energy - Highlighting Clean Energy Innovations in Upstate New York|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref> which received funding from both the Department of Energy and the National Science Foundation.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2018/11/ecolectro-receives-17m-doe-accelerate-hydrogen-fuel-development|title=Ecolectro receives $1.7M from DOE to accelerate hydrogen fuel development|publisher=[[Cornell Chronicle]]|date=November 30, 2018|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://nexus-ny.org/ecolectro/|title=eColectro Ready to Scale, Seeking Investors|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1548861|title=Award Abstract #1548861 - SBIR Phase I: Polymer electrolyte membrane synthesis to enable low cost, durable fuel cells through novel material innovation|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref>

== Research ==

Abruña develops materials to enhance [[fuel cell]] performance, in particular the [[Redox|oxygen reduction reaction]], and researches materials for battery applications.<ref name="Cornell Sun NAS" />

In 2016, Abruña developed a device that combines the large [[Energy storage|energy-storage]] capacity of [[Electric battery|batteries]] with the high charge-discharge rate of [[supercapacitor]]s. The technology is based on infusing an [[Conductive polymer|electronically conducting polymer]] [[thin film]] into a [[Covalent organic framework|covalent organic framework (COF)]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2016/08/best-both-worlds-team-proposes-novel-energy-storage-model|title=Best of both worlds: Team proposes novel energy storage model|publisher=[[Cornell Chronicle]]|date=August 31, 2016|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref> combining the COF's lightweight properties with the superior conductivity of the polymer.

Abruña also works on other electronics research.
In 2002, he collaborated on a project that created a single-atom [[transistor]] with [[Paul McEuen]] at Cornell.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.eetimes.com/cornell-demos-single-atom-transistor/|title=Cornell demos single-atom transistor|date=June 25, 2002|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.spacedaily.com/reports/The_Electrons_Are_Virtually_Dancing_At_The_Single_Atom_Club.html|title=The Electrons Are Virtually Dancing At The Single Atom Club|date=June 17, 2002|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref>
Abruña created extremely small light sources with sizes of only hundreds of nanometers by depositing light-emitting polymer fibers on a silicon substrate patterned with gold electrodes.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/2007/04/18/225939/tiny-light-bulbs/|title=Tiny Light Bulbs|publisher=[[MIT Technology Review]]|date=April 18, 2007|access-date=April 26, 2020}}</ref>
